name: Treaty with the Yankton Sioux, 1858
promises: A reservation of 400,000 acres on the Missouri River, beginning at the mouth of the Chouteau River, kept by the Yankton out of their cession (Article 1).
The United States to protect the Yankton in quiet and peaceable possession of the reservation, and in their persons and property there, during good behaviour (Article 4, First).

$1,600,000 in annuities over fifty years: $65,000 a year for ten years, $40,000 for ten, $25,000 for ten and $15,000 for twenty (Article 4, Second), plus $50,000 for subsistence, stock and improvements, $10,000 for schools and up to $15,000 for a mill and shops (Article 4).
Free and unrestricted use of the red pipestone quarry, which the United States was to survey, mark and keep open to the Yankton (Article 8).

breaches.what: The Indian Claims Commission found the Yankton interests ceded by this treaty (11,168,371 acres in Royce Area 410, worth $13,557,477, and a 7 per cent interest in the Sioux lands of the 1851 Fort Laramie treaty, worth $2,269,008.50) had a value of $15,826,485.50 when the treaty took effect on February 26, 1859, held the $1,662,500 the United States agreed to pay an unconscionable consideration, and awarded $15,269,924.83.

breaches.what: The Supreme Court held that the Yankton owned the pipestone quarry tract of about 648 acres in fee, that the United States had taken possession of the whole tract after Congress provided for an Indian school there in 1891, and that the Yankton were entitled to just compensation as for a taking under eminent domain.

landTaken: 11,168,371 acres in Royce Area 410, plus a 7 per cent interest in the 60,308,000-acre Sioux tract of the 1851 Fort Laramie treaty (Docket 332-C, 1978). The pipestone quarry tract of about 648 acres was taken separately after 1891 (272 U.S. 351).
compensation: Docket 332-C: $15,826,485.50 in value less payments on the claim of $556,560.67, a final award of $15,269,924.83 (August 31, 1978). For the quarry, the Supreme Court in 1926 held the Yankton entitled to just compensation without fixing the amount.
today: The claimant in Docket 332-C was the Yankton Sioux Tribe. The tribe also received $1,250,000 in a 1969 compromise in Docket 332-A for its Royce 151 claim under the 1830 treaty, a separate cession.

nationVoice.summary: In its 2011 filing to the Supreme Court the Tribe says the 1858 Treaty, under which it ceded more than 11 million acres and kept 430,405 acres, set the reservation's boundaries, and that everything inside them remains reservation except the 168,000 acres it sold to the United States in 1894.

openQuestions: Whether and how much the United States paid the Yankton for the quarry after the 1926 decision was not traced.
South Dakota v. Yankton Sioux Tribe (1998) concerned whether an 1894 act diminished this treaty's reservation; it was not opened here and is a lead for the reservation's later history.
The Yankton Sioux Tribe's own account of this treaty was not found online in this pass; its website showed no history page to an automated reader.
The pipestone quarry is a place of deep cultural importance; this record keeps only the legal facts of ownership and taking.
